hook: The world's fastest production jet, lighting up on a desert runway.
narration: The world's fastest production jet, lighting its afterburners on a desert runway.
This is NASA's SR-71 Blackbird, taking off from Edwards Air Force Base in 1991.
The Air Force built it as a spy plane that could cruise above eighty-five thousand feet.
It could top twenty-two hundred miles an hour, over three times the speed of sound.
At that speed the air heats the skin, so the Blackbird was built mostly from titanium.
NASA borrowed two and used them as flying laboratories.
[short pause] Its final flight came in October 1999. The next day, a fuel leak grounded it.
outcome: It never flew again, and NASA's Blackbirds went to museums.
title: SR-71 Blackbird takeoff, Mach 3 jet
description:
NASA's SR-71 Blackbird takes off from Edwards Air Force Base in California's Mojave Desert in 1991. NASA flew its loaned SR-71s for high-speed research until October 1999.

facts.claim: The video shows NASA's SR-71 taking off from Edwards AFB in 1991
facts.source_quote: This 43 seconds video from 1991 shows the NASA SR-71 taking off from Edwards Air Force Base in California's Mojave Desert.

facts.claim: Built as an Air Force reconnaissance aircraft, the world's fastest production aircraft
facts.source_quote: Developed for the U.S. Air Force as reconnaissance aircraft more than 30 years ago, SR-71 aircraft were the world's fastest and highest-flying production aircraft.
These aircraft could fly more than 2200 miles per hour (Mach 3+ or more than three times the speed of sound) and at altitudes of over 85,000 feet.

facts.claim: NASA borrowed two SR-71As for research, including lasers, sonic booms and a rocket engine
facts.source_quote: Two SR-71A aircraft were loaned from the U.S. Air Force for use for high-speed, high-altitude research at the NASA Dryden Flight Research Center

facts.claim: Last flight Oct. 9, 1999 at the air show; a fuel leak grounded it; storage then museums
facts.source_quote: The last SR-71 flight was made on Saturday October 9, 1999, at the Edwards AFB air show. The aircraft used was NASA 844. The aircraft was also scheduled to make a flight the following day, but a fuel leak grounded the aircraft and prevented it from flying again. The NASA SR-71s were then put in flyable storage, where they remained until 2002. They were then sent to museums.
